title: The UK is a cautionary tale for the U.S.
gist: Noah Smith argues the UK's stagnation is institutional, not cultural, and extracts six transferable lessons for the U.S.: NIMBY veto points, over-reliance on finance, abrupt austerity, direct state provision of essential services, cutting off export markets, and energy scarcity. He backs it with hard numbers — Brexit cutting UK GDP 6-8% and investment 12-13% by end-2025, HS2 costs tripling past £100bn, a 6-million-patient NHS backlog, and London's output accounting for 14% of British living standards.

insights.claim: Whether Britain's relative decline began in 2008 or in 2016 depends entirely on the deflator: using national price indices the UK has grown slower than the U.S. since the financial crisis, but on PPP prices — as Paul Krugman prefers — the stagnation only starts with Brexit.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The diagnosis of Britain's problem — financial-crisis scarring versus trade rupture — is deflator-dependent, so treat any single-cause UK decline narrative as a choice of measure, not a fact.
insights.locator: Whether you think the UK has been falling behind America economically

insights.claim: The UK's GDP per capita in PPP terms is roughly $56,000, about the same as Mississippi's, and the safety-and-health tradeoff does not explain it because France and Germany are at least as safe and healthy while being significantly richer.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Removes the standard defence of British living standards, which means the gap has to be explained by productivity and institutions — the things policy can actually move.
insights.locator: A data point that gets thrown around a lot

insights.claim: Resolution Foundation data show middle-income Britons are 20% poorer than German peers and 9% poorer than French ones, while low-income UK households are around 27% poorer than their French and German counterparts — a £4,300 gap for the lowest-income households versus France.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The UK shortfall is worst at the bottom of the distribution, which is where consumption-sensitive UK retail and consumer credit exposure sits.
insights.quote: Middle-income Brits are now 20 per cent poorer than their peers in Germany and 9 per cent poorer than those in France.
insights.locator: This is from a Resolution Foundation report

insights.claim: A deep economic principle holds that countries with roughly equivalent basic institutions should converge to similar income levels, so persistent UK-US divergence is itself evidence of specific British institutional weaknesses rather than bad luck.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Divergence-as-diagnostic gives a screening rule: where peer economies with similar institutions fail to converge, look for a specific institutional blocker rather than a cyclical story.
insights.quote: A very deep principle in economics is that if two countries are roughly equivalent in terms of their basic institutions, they ought to converge to similar income levels.
insights.locator: A very deep principle in economics

themes.theme: NIMBYism and the cost of building

insights.claim: HS2's costs have tripled since it was proposed in 2009 to more than £100 billion, making it the most expensive rail line in the world, and the truncated Birmingham-to-not-quite-central-London stub may not be finished until 2040.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A benchmark for infrastructure cost blowout risk: sponsors of megaprojects in permissive-veto jurisdictions should be underwritten at multiples of headline budget.
insights.locator: Recent plans to transform the country

insights.claim: Britain hosts the world's most expensive not-yet-built nuclear plant in Hinkley Point C, whose environmental-impact assessment ran 31,401 pages and which will include a £700 million acoustic 'fish disco' to deter animals from intake pipes.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Procedural compliance cost, not construction cost, is what makes Western nuclear uneconomic — the variable to watch in any nuclear-renaissance thesis is permitting reform, not reactor design.
insights.quote: Its environmental-impact assessment ran 31,401 pages; the plant will feature a £700 million “fish disco,”
insights.locator: Britain also hosts the world’s most expensive (not yet built) nuclear-power plant

insights.claim: Britain's housing crisis is worse than America's despite Britain having no zoning regime to speak of, because every attempt to build is instead a painful ad hoc negotiation with local councils and NIMBY residents.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Zoning reform alone does not fix housing supply; discretionary case-by-case permitting can be worse than rules-based zoning, which reframes what counts as a real YIMBY win.
insights.quote: The problem cannot even be blamed on zoning, because Britain does not have a zoning regime to speak of.
insights.locator: Britain suffers from a housing crisis significantly worse

insights.claim: France has roughly the same population as the UK but almost 50 percent more homes, and UK housing production has actually fallen since the financial crisis while housing costs per square foot are among the highest in Europe.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A structural supply deficit that is still widening supports persistently high UK housing costs and rents, and caps real disposable income growth.
insights.locator: France has roughly the same population as the U.K.

insights.claim: The typical house sold in London in 2024 cost 11 times median earnings, and one report concluded British housing stock offers the worst value for money of any advanced economy.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: An 11x price-to-earnings ratio in the country's only productive metro is a hard ceiling on labour mobility and therefore on UK productivity growth.
insights.quote: In London, the typical house sold in 2024 cost 11 times median earnings.
insights.locator: In London, the typical house sold in 2024

insights.claim: The transferable lesson from British paralysis is that approval policies full of veto points and cumbersome procedures drag on the economy, local control can easily go too far, and good infrastructure is a matter of low-cost efficiency rather than pure willingness to pay.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Cost-per-mile efficiency, not appropriations size, is the metric that determines whether US infrastructure spending converts into delivered assets — California's rail story rhymes with HS2's.
insights.locator: One of the key lessons here appears to be that NIMBYism kills

insights.claim: Removing London's output and headcount would shave 14 per cent off British living standards, enough to drop the rest of Britain behind the poorest US state — so the aggregate UK number is propped up entirely by one outlier capital.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: UK regional exposure outside London should be underwritten closer to emerging-market income levels than to headline UK GDP per capita.
insights.quote: Removing London’s output and headcount would shave 14 per cent off British living standards, precisely enough to slip behind the last of the US states.
insights.locator: John Burn-Murdoch writes

insights.claim: Financial services account for about 12% of UK economic output versus around 7% in the United States, with the City of London the world's second-largest asset management hub, the leading foreign-exchange venue and the number one location for over-the-counter derivatives.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The UK is effectively a levered bet on global financial activity; UK macro assets should be treated as correlated with financial-sector cycles, not diversified against them.
insights.locator: As Reuters reports, the UK economy specializes in finance

insights.claim: Because finance has an unusually strong clustering effect, hyper-financialization makes a country's financial capital the centre of its entire economy — so NIMBY-driven London housing scarcity bites harder by pricing workers out of participation in one of the few healthy parts of Britain's economy.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The housing and financialization problems compound rather than add, which means UK productivity fixes require solving both simultaneously to work at all.
insights.locator: Not only does this mean that the fruits of the UK economy

insights.claim: Specializing in a single tentpole industry left the UK unusually exposed to a crash in that industry, so the 2008 financial crisis and the follow-on Euro Crisis hit the whole economy — UK real wages stagnated and fell for years afterward while US average weekly earnings kept rising.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sector concentration is a sovereign-level risk factor: single-industry economies deserve a growth discount regardless of how profitable that industry currently is.
insights.locator: Another obvious downside of financialization

insights.claim: British taxation is at its highest level since World War II yet public services have deteriorated, with the NHS carrying a backlog of 6 million patients — almost a tenth of the population — waiting for treatment and now spending more on settling maternity-malpractice claims than on providing maternity care.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Record tax take with degrading service output means the UK has little fiscal headroom left to buy its way out — raising the odds of further real spending compression.
insights.quote: Taxation is at the highest level since World War II, yet public services have deteriorated.
insights.locator: Kahloon writes

insights.claim: British public-sector pay has compressed to the point that junior doctors struck for the 15th time in three years over salaries starting at just £38,800, while the median British civil servant earns £35,680.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Chronic public-sector pay disputes are a recurring source of UK service disruption and fiscal pressure, and a leading indicator of skilled-labour emigration.
insights.locator: Incomes can be shockingly low

insights.claim: Post-2008 UK austerity maintained day-to-day NHS operating funding only by cannibalizing the capital budget, producing crumbling buildings, mental-health patients housed in vermin-infested Victorian-era cells and parts of the NHS operating in decrepit portacabins.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Capex-first cuts are the most damaging form of austerity because the bill arrives a decade later — a pattern to watch in any state-run infrastructure or utility exposure.
insights.locator: Funding for day-to-day NHS operations was maintained

insights.claim: After UK austerity cuts to welfare benefits took effect, the share of children spending half their childhood or more in poverty jumped from about 14 percent to 23 percent, with doctors reporting increased cases of vitamin-deficiency diseases such as rickets and scurvy.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Human-capital damage of this scale is a multi-decade drag on future labour productivity, meaning austerity's fiscal savings can be negative in present-value terms.
insights.locator: After austerity cuts to welfare benefits took effect

insights.claim: America's debt problem is becoming unsustainable and fiscal austerity will be necessary, but it must be done gradually by restraining spending growth and raising taxes rather than by abruptly slashing government services and public works.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Positions for US fiscal consolidation as a base case, with the trade being the composition of adjustment — tax-and-slow-growth beneficiaries versus discretionary spending and public-works exposure.
insights.quote: We’re going to need to do fiscal austerity, but it’s important that we do it gradually
insights.locator: The U.S. needs to hear this lesson

insights.claim: The NHS's model of direct state provision of care controls costs in the short term and is cheaper than peer systems for roughly similar outcomes, but it subjects health capital spending to the whims of politics — which is why post-2008 UK disinvestment left the system visibly falling apart while other rich countries kept investing.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The case against state provision here is political fragility rather than inefficiency, which favours insurance-based models and the private providers that operate inside them.
insights.locator: Kahloon’s example of the NHS actually demonstrates another lesson

insights.claim: Under Hugo Chavez, Venezuela's government starved its own state-owned oil company of capital investment in order to fund a bonanza of government largesse, with disastrous results — the same failure mode as NHS capital disinvestment.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: State-owned enterprises face a structural bias toward under-investment because their capex is politically fungible with transfers — a discount factor for any national-champion or SOE exposure.
insights.locator: under Hugo Chavez, Veneuzela’s government starved

insights.claim: The lesson that government provision is dangerous because it is inherently political rather than inherently inefficient is applied directly to socialists like Zohran Mamdani who promise to run essential services through the government.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Municipal experiments in state-run essential services are a live US political risk to incumbent private operators — and, on this argument, a chronic under-investment risk to the services themselves.
insights.quote: It’s not necessarily that government is inherently inefficient; it’s that it’s inherently political.
insights.locator: We should remember this when socialists like Zohran Mamdani

insights.claim: Bloom et al. (2025) estimate that by the end of 2025 Brexit had reduced UK GDP by 6% to 8%, investment by 12% to 13%, and both employment and productivity by 3% to 4%, with the impact accumulating steadily over time.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A hard magnitude for the cost of severing trade ties with a neighbouring bloc — the reference number to apply when pricing any deliberate trade rupture.
insights.quote: [B]y the end of 2025 Brexit had reduced UK GDP by 6% to 8%, with the impact accumulating steadily over time.
insights.locator: Bloom et al. (2025) study the growth impact of Brexit

insights.claim: The channels through which Brexit did its damage were elevated uncertainty, reduced demand, diverted management time and increased misallocation of resources from a protracted process — not just tariffs.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Prolonged policy uncertainty destroys investment even before any rules change, so the timeline of a trade dispute matters as much as its terms.
insights.quote: These negative impacts reflect a combination of elevated uncertainty, reduced demand, diverted management time, and increased misallocation of resources from a protracted Brexit process.
insights.locator: Bloom et al. (2025) study the growth impact of Brexit

insights.claim: Exports are over 30% of UK GDP versus only 11% in the U.S., so trade wars with allies would hurt America less than Brexit hurt Britain — but local multiplier effects mean even that smaller export stream supports a lot of domestic industry.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sets an upper bound on US tariff-war damage relative to the Brexit benchmark while warning that the multiplier makes the hit larger than the raw 11% export share implies.
insights.locator: The pre-Brexit UK was a more internationalized economy

themes.theme: Energy abundance as a growth input

insights.claim: High energy costs make British industry uncompetitive and thereby increase the country's reliance on finance, while also directly impoverishing households who consume far less energy per capita than people in other rich countries.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Energy cost is upstream of industrial competitiveness and of sector concentration, so power prices are a leading indicator for deindustrialization trades.
insights.locator: High energy costs help make British industry uncompetitive

insights.claim: Britain's energy scarcity is tied to an overly rapid and haphazard decarbonization push: having banned coal, and with natural gas made extremely expensive by the Ukraine war, the UK was forced to rely on hideously expensive offshore wind.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sequencing matters in energy transitions — retiring baseload before cheap replacements exist raises system costs, a repeatable failure mode to screen European utilities against.
insights.locator: The Economist ties Britain’s energy scarcity

insights.claim: There is no such thing as a low-energy rich country, and the U.S. escape route is solar plus batteries — much cheaper than offshore wind and getting cheaper — which makes MAGA opposition to solar power even more foolish than Britain's haphazard coal ban.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames US anti-solar policy as a self-inflicted growth constraint, making domestic solar-and-storage policy risk a macro variable rather than just a sector one.
insights.quote: there is no such thing as a low-energy rich country
insights.locator: But the general lesson remains

insights.claim: The UK, caught up in endless political turmoil and culture wars, has forgotten the overriding importance of growth for national happiness and well-being — and the U.S., facing its own political chaos, is at risk of repeating the mistake.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Political attention shifting from growing the pie to dividing it is the observable precursor to stagnation — a regime indicator for country allocation decisions.
insights.quote: countries turn away from growth at their peril
insights.locator: Overall, the UK should serve as a reminder

insights.claim: One diagnosis of Britain is a 'high-level equilibrium trap' in which a country stays wealthy enough that its politics centre on dividing the pie rather than growing it, while a rival account blames financialization rather than over-regulation for weak investment.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Competing diagnoses imply different trades — deregulation-and-build plays versus investment-and-industrial-policy plays — so watch which framework UK policymakers actually adopt.
insights.locator: There are a number of good breakdowns of the UK’s problems
